This streamlined process improves security and eliminates wait times when joining the call. ABOUT WM WM ( WM.com ) is North America's leading provider of comprehensive environmental solutions. Previously known as Waste Management and based in Houston, Texas, WM is driven by commitments to put people first and achieve success with integrity. The company, through its subsidiaries, provides collection, recycling and disposal services to millions of residential, commercial, industrial, medical and municipal customers throughout the U.S. and Canada. With innovative infrastructure and capabilities in recycling, organics and renewable energy, WM provides environmental solutions to and collaborates with its customers in helping them pursue their sustainability goals. WM has the largest disposal network and collection fleet in North America, is the largest recycler of post-consumer materials and is a leader in beneficial use of landfill gas, with a growing network of renewable natural gas plants and the most landfill gas-to-electricity plants in North America. WM's fleet includes more than 12,000 natural gas trucks – the largest heavy-duty natural gas truck fleet in the industry in North America. Healthcare Solutions provides collection and disposal services of regulated medical waste, as well as secure information destruction services, in the U.S., Canada and Western Europe. To learn more about WM and the company's sustainability progress and solutions, visit Sustainability.WM.com . title: Vericel Announces Preliminary 2025 Financial Results and Business Updates
summary: The Investor Relations website contains information about Vericel Corporation's business for stockholders, potential investors, and financial analysts.
body_text: Investor Relations Press Releases Vericel Announces Preliminary 2025 Financial Results and Business Updates January 13, 2026 at 9:00 AM EST PDF Version Total Revenue Expected to be $276 Million MACI Revenue Expected to be $239.5 Million Fourth Quarter Total Revenue and MACI Revenue Growth of 23% CAMBRIDGE, Mass., Jan. 13, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Vericel Corporation (NASDAQ:VCEL), a leader in advanced therapies for the sports medicine and severe burn care markets, today announced preliminary, unaudited financial results and other business updates for the fourth quarter and year ended December 31, 2025. Preliminary, Unaudited Full-Year 2025 Financial Results Total net revenue expected to be approximately $276 million, with MACI® net revenue of $239.5 million and Burn Care net revenue of $36.5 million Gross margin expected to be 74% and adjusted EBITDA margin expected to be 26% GAAP Net Income profitability expected for the second consecutive year $200 million in cash and investments, and no debt Business Highlights and Updates Highest number of MACI implants, implanting surgeons, surgeons taking biopsies and MACI biopsies in any quarter since launch in the fourth quarter MACI revenue growth of 20% or more for the third consecutive year Completed MACI sales force expansion More than 900 MACI Arthro® trained surgeons as of year-end 2025 Initiated MACI Ankle™ MASCOT clinical study Remain on track to begin MACI commercial manufacturing in new facility in 2026 “The Company executed extremely well in 2025, delivering strong revenue and profitability growth,” said Nick Colangelo, President and CEO of Vericel. “We are entering 2026 with a great deal of momentum and expect another year of high revenue growth, increasing MACI utilization and further growth in profitability and cash generation as we continue to progress toward our mid-term financial targets.” Vericel is scheduled to present at the 44th Annual J.P. Morgan Healthcare Conference at 2:15 p.m. ET (11:15 a.m. PT) on Wednesday, January 14, 2026. A webcast of the presentation will be available on the Investor Relations section of the Vericel Corporation website at: http://investors.vcel.com . About Vericel Corporation Vericel is a leading provider of advanced therapies for the sports medicine and severe burn care markets. The Company combines innovations in biology with medical technologies, resulting in a highly differentiated portfolio of innovative cell therapies and specialty biologics that repair injuries and restore lives. Vericel markets three products in the United States. MACI (autologous cultured chondrocytes on porcine collagen membrane) is an autologous cellularized scaffold product indicated for the repair of symptomatic, single or multiple full-thickness cartilage defects of the knee with or without bone involvement in adults. Epicel® (cultured epidermal autografts) is a permanent skin replacement for the treatment of patients with deep dermal or full thickness burns greater than or equal to 30% of total body surface area. Vericel also holds an exclusive license for North American rights to NexoBrid (anacaulase-bcdb), a biological orphan product containing proteolytic enzymes, which is indicated for eschar removal in adults and pediatric patients with deep partial-thickness and/or full-thickness thermal burns. For more information, please visit www.vcel.com . Epicel®, MACI® and MACI Arthro® are registered trademarks of Vericel Corporation. NexoBrid® is a registered trademark of MediWound Ltd. and is used under license to Vericel Corporation. © 2026 Vericel Corporation. All rights reserved. Preliminary and Unaudited Nature of Reported Results Our revenue expectations for the fourth quarter and full-year ended 2025, as well as our estimates concerning net income, gross margin, adjusted EBITDA margin and cash and investments are preliminary, unaudited and are subject to change based on the completion of ongoing internal control, review, and audit procedures. As a result, these amounts may differ materially from the amounts that will be reflected in the Company’s consolidated financial statements for the year ended December 31, 2025. Accordingly, you should not place undue reliance on this preliminary estimate. GAAP v. Non-GAAP Measures Vericel’s expected and reported earnings are prepared in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles in the United States, or GAAP, and represent earnings as reported to the Securities and Exchange Commission. Vericel has provided in this release certain financial information that has not been prepared in accordance with GAAP. Vericel’s management believes that the non-GAAP adjusted EBITDA margin described in this release, which includes adjustments for specific items that are generally not indicative of our core operations, provides additional information that is useful to investors in understanding Vericel’s underlying performance, business and performance trends, and helps facilitate period-to-period comparisons and comparisons of its financial measures with other companies in Vericel’s industry. However, the non-GAAP financial measures that Vericel uses may differ from measures that other companies may use. title: Why Medicare Retention Fails After Enrollment (And What Agencies Can Do About It)
summary: Most Medicare retention programs fail after enrollment because nothing learns from member conversations. Here’s why retention breaks downand what agencies can do to reduce churn year-round.
body_text: careCycle exists for a simple reason: Medicare agencies lose members after enrollment, and most don’t realize it until it’s too late. Not because their agents are underperforming. Not because their sales process is broken. But because once enrollment is complete, almost nothing meaningful happens next. Retention doesn’t fail at renewal. It fails in the quiet months after enrollment, when questions go unanswered, confusion compounds, and trust slowly erodes. The Moment Most Systems Shut Off Most Medicare infrastructure is built around events: lead intake, enrollment, AEP. Once the application is submitted, the system relaxes. A welcome packet is sent. An onboarding email goes out. The assumption is that stability follows until renewal. careCycle was built after analyzing real post-enrollment behavior across nearly one million Medicare conversations and realizing that assumption is wrong. Members don’t stop needing help after enrollment. In many cases, that’s when questions actually begin. Prescription coverage confusion. Provider access. Billing issues. Benefit interpretation. Changes in health status. These aren’t exceptions. They’re the day-to-day reality of being a Medicare beneficiary. And critically, a meaningful share of these moments happen: After hours Outside scripted flows Under emotional stress This is where retention is actually decided. Why Most Medicare Retention Programs Don’t Adapt Most retention programs are static by design. They rely on scheduled outreach instead of real-time demand. Scripts instead of context. CRMs that store notes but never surface patterns. Human agents repeatedly solving the same problems in isolation. From the outside, it looks like effort. From the inside, it’s stagnation. The same questions show up month after month. The same confusion resurfaces every AEP. The same issues reach human agents again and again. But the system never improves, because it has no mechanism to learn from what’s happening at scale. careCycle was designed specifically to close that gap. Retention Isn’t About More Touchpoints. It’s About Learning. The most common mistake agencies make is assuming retention improves with volume: more calls, more check-ins, more campaigns. In reality, retention improves with feedback loops . When we looked across hundreds of thousands of post-enrollment conversations, the strongest outcomes didn’t come from agencies working harder. They came from systems that observed patterns, adapted workflows, and improved with every interaction. Every repeated question is a signal. Every escalation reveals friction. Every confused caller points to something upstream that can be fixed. careCycle treats post-enrollment conversations as intelligence, not noise. Why Voice Is the Missing Layer in Medicare Retention Post-enrollment Medicare conversations are rarely clean or predictable. Members change topics mid-sentence. They interrupt themselves. They express frustration without stating it directly. Voice captures what structured systems miss: Tone and hesitation Emotional escalation Repeated confusion across different members Where conversations break down, not just where they end This matters because Medicare retention is emotional before it is transactional. When voice systems are designed properly, members don’t disengage when they realize they’re speaking to AI. In fact, many express appreciation mid-conversation and complete interactions naturally without requesting a human transfer. That doesn’t happen in systems that feel robotic or transactional. It happens when voice is used to support, not deflect. careCycle’s voice layer is built for this reality. It handles routine questions, escalates intelligently, preserves full context, and feeds what it learns back into the system so the next interaction is better than the last. Static Retention Programs vs Learning Systems Most Medicare retention programs ask: Was the member contacted? Did someone answer the call? Was the issue closed? careCycle asks different questions: Why did this issue arise in the first place? How often is it happening across the book? Should this be automated, clarified, or prevented entirely? What should change before the next member calls? That difference compounds over time. Instead of agents repeatedly solving the same problems, the system improves upstream. Instead of entering every AEP scrambling to replace lost members, agencies show up with a healthier, more engaged book. In production deployments, AI-human hybrid workflows consistently resolve complex Medicare inquiries while preserving compliance and escalation controls. The result isn’t fewer agents. It’s more capacity, less burnout, and better member experiences at scale. Why careCycle Focuses on Post-Enrollment careCycle supports the entire Medicare lifecycle, from first conversation through renewal. That includes sales. Enrollment matters. Getting the decision right matters. But where most systems stop at the close, careCycle keeps working. The reality of Medicare is that sales is an event. Retention is a system. Once enrollment is complete, the questions start. Benefits get used. Prescriptions change. Providers matter. Life happens. These moments rarely show up in sales dashboards, but they ultimately determine whether a member stays, disengages, or leaves at renewal. That’s why careCycle is built to extend beyond enrollment and into the long middle — the months where trust is either reinforced or quietly lost. AI in this context isn’t about replacing agents or automating away relationships. It’s about supporting them across the full lifecycle. Absorbing routine demand. Preserving context between conversations. Making sure licensed agents step in with clarity, not cold starts. Sales opens the relationship. Post-enrollment determines its value. By treating enrollment and retention as one continuous system — not disconnected workflows — careCycle helps agencies scale both growth and longevity without breaking their teams. That’s how Medicare books compound instead of resetting every October. Retention Is a System, Not a Campaign Agencies don’t rebuild their book every October because Medicare is seasonal. They rebuild because nothing compounds the rest of the year. If your post-enrollment system doesn’t learn, retention flatlines. If every conversation makes the system smarter, retention compounds. That’s the shift careCycle was built to enable. And it’s why agencies that stop treating retention like a renewal problem start seeing it for what it really is: an infrastructure advantage.

Investors are adding Platinum to their portfolios for four reasons: a historic valuation gap, a resurgence in auto demand, future green energy tech, and a supply chain that is hanging by a thread. 1. The Valuation Gap Historically, Platinum was more expensive than Gold (trading at ~$2,200/oz in 2008). Today, it trades at a historic discount to Gold. Value investors view this ratio as unsustainable. If Platinum merely reverts to its historical mean relative to Gold, the price upside is significant, regardless of what the broader market does. The metal has already started moving up, with a ~50% gain noted in the first half of 2025. 2. Auto Demand For years, automakers used Palladium for catalytic converters because it was cheaper. When Palladium prices spiked, they spent billions retooling factories to switch back to Platinum. That retooling is now complete. Demand from the auto sector is sticky and rising. 3. As Europe and the Middle East move large-scale green hydrogen projects from "planning" to "operation" in 2026, industrial demand is creating a new price floor. It is no longer just a jewelry metal; it is a green energy metal. 4. The South African Choke Point ~75% of the world's platinum comes from South Africa. The supply chain is incredibly fragile due to aging mines, labor strikes, and the ongoing electricity crisis (Eskom) in the region. summary: Understand women’s libido and the factors influencing sex drive. Explore common causes for low desire, lifestyle tips to improve libido, and when to seek professional primary care.
body_text: Women’s Libido: What’s Normal, What’s Not, and How to Improve Libido TL;DR: How to Increase Libido in Women Low sex drive in women is common and often reflects physical health, emotional well-being, hormones, stress, and relationship factors, not willpower or failure. Libido is not a single switch. Sexual desire involves arousal, emotional connection, comfort, and overall sexual satisfaction, all of which can change across life stages. Hormonal shifts, stress, medications, medical conditions, and emotional or relationship concerns are common reasons libido may drop. Lifestyle changes such as regular exercise, balanced nutrition, adequate sleep, stress management, and emotional connection can naturally support a healthy libido. Persistent low libido that causes personal distress, painful sex, vaginal dryness, or fatigue may signal an underlying health issue worth evaluating. Primary care can help by looking at the full picture , including physical health, mental health, medications, and lifestyle, and supporting personalized next steps. Why Low Libido Happens: Understanding the Bigger Picture Sexual desire in women reflects physical health, emotional well-being, hormones, relationships, and daily stressors and not just willpower or motivation alone . Sexual desire, sex drive, and libido are often used interchangeably, and many women experience periods of low sexual desire at different points in life. If sex drive feels lower than usual, many women worry that something is “wrong.” In reality, libido often shifts when the body or mind is carrying more: whether that is stress, fatigue, discomfort, or a change in hormones. Many women notice changes in sex drive during specific life stages, such as postpartum recovery, prolonged periods of stress, perimenopause, or menopause. These changes are common and expected because libido responds to sleep, energy levels, emotional load, physical comfort, and hormonal balance. Understanding how libido works, and what truly supports women’s sexual health, allows women to make informed, compassionate choices about their bodies. A healthy libido is not defined by frequency or performance. A healthy libido is about comfort, connection, and sexual satisfaction within a woman’s own life, relationships, and values. Why Libido Is Not a Single Switch in Women Libido includes interest, sexual arousal, emotional closeness, and sexual satisfaction, which are all core components of female sexual function and overall sexual health. These elements rise and fall naturally across menstrual cycles, life transitions, and changing stress levels because the body prioritizes energy, safety, and well-being. Short-term drops in sexual desire are common among many women, and they often improve as sleep, stress, physical comfort, emotional health, and other lifestyle factors improve. If low libido becomes persistent or starts to feel distressing, the next step is not self-blame. A persistent change can be a helpful clue that physical health, mental health, medications, or relationship factors deserve a closer look. When Libido Drops: Common Reasons in Women Hormonal changes influence sexual desire Estrogen and testosterone both play roles in women’s sexual health, sexual arousal, and genital blood flow, influencing comfort, sensitivity, and desire. When estrogen levels drop, such as during perimenopause or menopause, vaginal tissues can become thinner and drier. During postpartum recovery, especially while breastfeeding, lower estrogen levels can also contribute to vaginal dryness and sensitivity. Vaginal dryness and painful intercourse can make sex uncomfortable, so it makes sense when desire drops in response . Hormonal birth control can also influence libido for some women by altering hormone balance, particularly in premenopausal women, though responses vary widely. These effects vary widely, and they depend on factors like individual biology, dosage, and overall health history. Chronic stress reduces sexual desire Ongoing stress raises cortisol levels, which can interfere with sexual arousal, emotional presence, and genital blood flow, a relationship observed in clinical and physiological research on stress and sexual response . Mental load, caregiving responsibilities, work pressure, and relationship strain commonly affect women’s sex drive, even when attraction and intimacy are still present. Stress-related low desire is not a personal failing. Stress-related low desire is the nervous system doing its job, prioritizing survival and recovery when life feels demanding. Medical conditions and medications affect libido Thyroid disorders, diabetes, high blood pressure, chronic pain, mood disorders, liver disorders, and other underlying health conditions can influence sexual function, energy levels, and overall women’s health. Women taking antidepressants may notice changes in libido, arousal, sexual satisfaction, or other sexual concerns, which can sometimes be addressed through medication review. Some medications affect blood flow, nerve signaling, or hormone balance. Reviewing medications with a primary care provider can help determine whether adjustments or alternatives should be considered. Emotional and relationship factors shape desire Relationship stress, unresolved conflict, body image concerns, and low self-esteem can reduce sexual intimacy and responsiveness. Desire often improves when emotional needs are acknowledged, communication feels safer, and pressure is reduced. Libido is closely linked to emotional well-being, not just physical readiness for a sexual encounter. Feeling emotionally safe and supported often makes it easier for desire to show up. How Lifestyle Changes Can Improve Libido in Women Exercise improves libido through blood flow and mood Exercise increases blood flow throughout the body, including genital tissues, which supports sexual arousal, genital arousal, and physical responsiveness. Exercise improves sexual function by supporting circulation, mood, and energy. Aerobic activity supports cardiovascular health and stamina, while strength training and pelvic floor exercises help maintain muscle tone and support sexual function. Mind-body movement such as yoga or Pilates supports nervous system regulation and body awareness. These forms of movement can help women feel more present and comfortable in their bodies, which often enhances sexual satisfaction. Exercise Types and Libido-Related Benefits Exercise Type Examples How It Supports Libido Aerobic exercise Brisk walking, jogging, cycling, swimming Improves cardiovascular health and blood flow, including genital blood flow, which supports sexual arousal and overall sexual function. Also boosts mood and energy. Strength training Weight lifting, resistance bands, bodyweight exercises Builds muscle strength and endurance, supports healthy hormone balance, and can improve body confidence, which may positively influence sex drive. Pelvic floor exercises Kegels, guided pelvic floor training Strengthens pelvic muscles involved in arousal and orgasm, supports sexual comfort, and may improve sexual satisfaction. Mind-body movement Yoga, Pilates, tai chi Helps regulate the nervous system, reduce stress, and increase body awareness, supporting emotional comfort and sexual responsiveness. Nutrition supports hormone balance and energy Healthy fats support hormone production, protein supports neurotransmitters involved in desire, and micronutrients such as zinc, magnesium, and omega-3 fatty acids play important roles in sexual health. Eating regular, balanced meals also helps stabilize blood sugar, which supports steady energy and mood. Limiting too much alcohol can support a healthy libido, emotional well-being, and overall physical and mental health. Excess alcohol and illegal drugs can negatively affect sexual function and desire. While many supplements are marketed as a natural libido booster, evidence varies. Nutrition-focused lifestyle changes tend to provide more reliable, long-term benefits for women’s sexual health. Key Nutrients That Support Libido and Sexual Health Nutrient Why It Matters for Libido Food Examples Healthy fats Support hormone production and vaginal tissue health, which can influence comfort and sexual desire Avocado, olive oil, nuts, seeds Protein Supports neurotransmitters involved in mood, motivation, and sexual desire Eggs, poultry, fish, beans, tofu Zinc Plays a role in hormone balance and sexual function Oysters, beef, pumpkin seeds, chickpeas Magnesium Supports muscle relaxation, stress regulation, and energy levels Leafy greens, nuts, seeds, whole grains Omega-3 fatty acids Support blood flow, cardiovascular health, and nervous system function Fatty fish (salmon, sardines), flaxseed, walnuts Sleep restores hormones and desire Sleep deprivation can disrupt stress hormones and the hormonal systems that support mood, energy, and sexual function, which may reduce sexual interest and physical arousal. Ongoing fatigue also lowers emotional bandwidth for intimacy, especially for women managing caregiving responsibilities, work demands, or irregular schedules. Stress management supports arousal Mindfulness, breathing exercises, gentle routines, and intentional rest can reduce cortisol levels and support emotional availability. When stress feels more manageable, many women notice that desire and responsiveness return more easily, without needing to force the issue. Emotional connection strengthens sexual desire Open communication, affection, and shared experiences strengthen emotional connection, sexual intimacy, and relationship satisfaction, all of which support a healthy libido. Sexual intimacy includes presence, trust, and mutual understanding, not just sexual activity. When Low Libido Signals an Underlying Health Issue Medical care can be helpful when low libido is ongoing, recurrent, or accompanied by symptoms such as sexual pain, painful sex, vaginal dryness, painful intercourse, mood changes, fatigue, or other shifts in physical or emotional health. In these situations, low desire may be a signal of an underlying health condition rather than a standalone sexual concern. A primary care evaluation focuses on understanding the full picture. Blood tests may be considered when hormonal changes, thyroid conditions, testosterone levels, estrogen levels drop, or other medical factors are suspected, helping guide next steps with clarity and care. What a Primary Care Evaluation for Low Libido Looks Like A primary care evaluation is designed to understand what may be influencing libido, not to reduce the experience to a single cause. Many women find it helpful to talk through symptoms, sleep quality, stress levels, medications, sexual history, mental health, emotional well-being, and relationship factors with a clinician who can connect the dots, along with a review of overall health. Lab testing may be considered when appropriate to assess hormone levels or rule out underlying health conditions. Care plans are individualized and focus on realistic, supportive next steps. These may include lifestyle guidance, addressing medical conditions, adjusting medications when appropriate, or discussing hormone-related care if clinically indicated. Hormone therapy, including vaginal estrogen for some postmenopausal women with vaginal dryness or painful sex, is not appropriate for everyone and requires careful evaluation, shared decision-making, and ongoing monitoring. How Accessible Primary Care Can Support Women’s Sexual Health Circle Medical provides accessible primary care for libido concerns Circle Medical makes it easier for women to seek care for libido concerns in a supportive, low-pressure setting. Through virtual and in-person primary care appointments, providers take time to listen, understand what has changed, and consider physical health, emotional well-being, medications, and lifestyle factors that may be influencing sexual health. Primary care doctors focus on identifying contributing factors, answering questions, and helping guide thoughtful next steps. When additional support is needed, care coordination and follow-up help ensure women feel supported, informed, and not navigating concerns alone. Common Questions About Low Libido in Women Can exercise really increase libido in women? Yes. Regular exercise can support libido by improving circulation, mood, energy levels, and overall physical comfort. Aerobic activity supports blood flow and cardiovascular health, while strength training and mind-body movement can improve body awareness and confidence, factors that often contribute to sexual desire and satisfaction. Does low libido always mean a hormone problem? No. While hormones play a role, low libido often reflects a combination of factors such as stress, sleep quality, medications, mental health, relationship dynamics, and overall physical well-being. Hormonal changes are one possible contributor, but they are not the only explanation. When should I talk to a doctor about low libido? It may be helpful to talk with a primary care provider if low libido is persistent, causes personal distress, or does not improve with lifestyle changes. Medical care is also appropriate when low desire occurs alongside symptoms such as pain during sex, vaginal dryness, mood changes, or fatigue. Can primary care help with sexual health concerns? Yes. Primary care providers can evaluate the physical, emotional, and lifestyle factors that influence sexual health. They help identify possible contributing causes, recommend appropriate next steps, and coordinate care when additional support is needed. When Libido Changes, Whole-Person Care Matters Female libido reflects whole-person health, not a single fix or failure. Changes in desire often make sense when viewed alongside sleep, stress, emotional well-being, physical comfort, and overall health. Lifestyle changes, emotional support, and medical guidance can all play meaningful roles in helping desire return in a way that feels sustainable and aligned with a woman’s life. When questions or concerns persist, primary care offers a supportive starting point for understanding what your body may be communicating. If low libido is affecting your quality of life, a Circle Medical provider can help evaluate potential contributing factors and support a personalized care plan, at a pace that feels comfortable and collaborative.
